generatedProse.concept-context: Passive revision is common across the School of Sport because there is so much to take in: coaching theories, session models, physiology summaries and lecture notes. Reading them again feels productive, but it only builds recognition. Active revision makes you produce the knowledge instead. You recall a coaching model from memory, explain a principle of training in your own words, sketch the phases of a session plan, or work through a practice problem. That effort of retrieval and application is what you will need in the exam.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students sit down to revise the same topic, a model of skill acquisition, for two hours.

Tom reads through his notes on the model, highlights the key stages, and reads them again. By the end the pages look well used and the model feels familiar. But Tom has only recognised it, not produced it. Asked to describe the model the next day, he can picture the diagram in his notes but cannot quite reconstruct it. This is passive review.

Amara reads her notes once, then closes them. She draws the model from memory, checks what she left out, turns the gaps into questions, and answers a short problem that applies the model to a coaching session. It feels harder and slower. But the next day she can reproduce the model and use it, because the effort of retrieving it is what fixed it. This is active revision.

Both students spent two hours. Only Amara made the knowledge retrievable, by recreating and applying it rather than re-reading it.
generatedProse.summary: Active revision beats passive review across the School of Sport because it makes you recreate or apply knowledge rather than take it in again. Re-reading session models and physiology summaries builds recognition; recalling a coaching model, explaining a training principle and working practice problems build the retrieval an exam demands. You can now tell the two apart and swap a passive habit for an active one. The next lesson gives you a toolkit of active techniques to choose from.

check.body: In the worked example, what was the active move Amara made instead of re-reading?

items.text: She closed her notes, drew the skill acquisition model from memory, and checked what she had missed.
She read her notes on the model more carefully than Tom did.
She highlighted the stages of the model first.
She spent longer on her notes than Tom did.

feedback.correct: That's right. Drawing the model from memory and checking it is active revision in action.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that made Amara produce the model, not re-read it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The active move was to close the notes, draw the model from memory, and check the gaps. Reading more carefully, highlighting or spending longer are all still passive.
